mechanisms.conditioning_logic: Condition on the joint ratio of shots-for to shots-on-target for each team simultaneously (not just one team's mirror), comparing Team A's all-prior ratio against its recent-5 ratio, and Team B's all-prior ratio against its recent-5 ratio, to detect whether a divergence in shot quality (shots-on-target per shot) between the two sides is associated with a differential in goals-for relative to shots-on-target.
mechanisms.expected_relationship_to_test: When one team's shots-on-target-per-shot ratio is substantially lower than the opponent's, goals-for relative to shots-on-target is suppressed for the lower-ratio team, even as raw shot volume rises.
mechanisms.mechanism_statement: Team A generates a high volume of shots and shots on target but converts at a rate that, when jointly examined with Team B's low shots-for but improving recent shots-for trend, reveals an asymmetric shot-volume-to-on-target ratio relationship between the two sides. Specifically, the joint pattern of Team A's shots-for versus shots-on-target ratio (both all-prior and recent) compared against Team B's equivalent ratio tests whether high shot volume without proportional on-target accuracy is associated with suppressed goal output relative to shot count.
mechanisms.why_not_baseline_equivalent: This requires a joint relationship across three observables (shots, shots_on_target, goals) for both teams simultaneously, comparing ratios across two time windows. It is not reducible to a single observable mirror or a single observable with one coarse band.

mechanisms.conditioning_logic: Jointly condition on both teams' possession levels and shots-for levels simultaneously. Specifically, test whether the team with lower possession (Team B, ~46%) but a recent surge in shots-for (9.6 all-prior to 14.2 recent) achieves a shots-on-target rate per possession unit that rises relative to the possession-dominant team (Team A, ~54-60% possession).
mechanisms.expected_relationship_to_test: The team with lower possession but a rising shots-for trend generates shots-on-target per possession unit at a rate that rises relative to the possession-dominant team, indicating a non-linear relationship between possession share and shot quality.
mechanisms.mechanism_statement: Team A holds substantially more possession than Team B (both all-prior and recent), while Team B's recent shots-for has surged relative to its all-prior average despite lower possession. This joint relationship between possession dominance and shot generation tests whether a team that cedes possession but increases shot volume (a counter-attacking profile) generates shots-on-target at a disproportionately higher rate per unit of possession than the possession-dominant team.
mechanisms.why_not_baseline_equivalent: This is a genuine joint relationship across two distinct observables (possession and shots/shots_on_target) for both teams simultaneously, not a single observable mirror or a single observable with one coarse band. The cross-team asymmetry in possession vs. shot-volume trends is the key structural feature.

mechanisms.conditioning_logic: Jointly condition on both the half-period (first vs second) and the team role (Team A scoring, Team B conceding), examining the cross-product of Team A's half-split goals-for with Team B's half-split goals-against. This is a two-dimensional conditioning: half-period × team-role asymmetry, not a single team's half split in isolation.
mechanisms.expected_relationship_to_test: The combination of Team A's second-half scoring surge and Team B's first-half defensive weakness produces a within-match goal distribution that is skewed differently than either team's individual half-split would predict in isolation — specifically, the first half may see more Team B vulnerability while the second half sees more Team A dominance.
mechanisms.mechanism_statement: Team A scores more goals in the second half than the first half (0.831 first half vs 1.169 second half), while Team B concedes more in the first half than the second half (0.75 first half vs 0.594 second half). This cross-team, cross-half asymmetry in goal timing tests whether the joint pattern of Team A's second-half scoring tendency and Team B's first-half defensive vulnerability produces a non-uniform within-match goal distribution that differs from what either team's full-match average alone would suggest.
mechanisms.why_not_baseline_equivalent: This requires simultaneously conditioning on two distinct dimensions: the half-period split AND the cross-team asymmetry between Team A's scoring half-distribution and Team B's conceding half-distribution. It is not a single observable's half split for one team.

mechanisms.conditioning_logic: Jointly condition on both teams' foul rates and Team A's recent yellow card surge, examining whether the combination of Team B's foul-committing tendency (11.656 all-prior, 9.8 recent) and Team A's elevated recent yellow card rate (3.0 recent vs 1.815 all-prior) is associated with elevated second-half card counts (cards_2h) beyond the competition context baseline of 1.167.
mechanisms.expected_relationship_to_test: When a team's own recent yellow card rate has surged AND the opponent commits fouls at an above-average rate, second-half card accumulation (cards_2h) rises above what either team's individual card or foul rate alone would predict — a joint amplification effect.
mechanisms.mechanism_statement: Team A's yellow cards have surged in recent matches (1.815 all-prior to 3.0 recent) while Team B commits more fouls per match than Team A allows (11.656 vs 10.769). The joint relationship between foul rate and second-half card accumulation tests whether a high-fouling opponent combined with a team's own elevated recent yellow card rate produces a non-linear escalation in second-half cards (cards_2h) beyond what either team's individual card or foul rate alone would predict.
mechanisms.why_not_baseline_equivalent: This involves a genuine joint relationship across three distinct observables (fouls, yellow_cards, cards_2h) with a within-match period split (second half) and a cross-team asymmetry. It is not reducible to a single observable mirror or a single coarse band.

mechanisms.conditioning_logic: Jointly condition on the half-period split (first vs second half) for corner kicks AND the possession level of Team A, examining whether Team A's possession dominance (especially its recent surge to 60.6%) interacts with the second-half escalation in both Team A's corners-for and Team B's corners-against to produce a non-additive increase in second-half corner totals.
mechanisms.expected_relationship_to_test: When a possession-dominant team's possession share rises in recent matches, its second-half corner generation escalates at a rate that exceeds the first-half rate, and this is amplified when the opponent's corner-conceding rate also rises in the second half — producing a super-additive second-half corner total relative to the first half.
mechanisms.mechanism_statement: Team A earns more corners in the second half than the first half (2.4 first half vs 2.6 second half for-corners), while Team B concedes more corners in the second half than the first half (2.125 first half vs 2.958 second half against-corners). Jointly conditioning on possession dominance (Team A ~54% all-prior, ~60% recent) and the half-period split of corner generation tests whether possession-dominant teams that increase their corner rate in the second half face opponents whose corner-conceding rate also escalates in the second half, producing a non-linear amplification of second-half corner totals beyond what full-match averages suggest.
mechanisms.why_not_baseline_equivalent: This requires jointly conditioning on two distinct observables (possession and corner_kicks) with a within-match half-period split and a cross-team asymmetry in half-distributions. It is not a single observable's half split or a single observable with one coarse band.
